title: What you knew, and when you knew it.
dek: Most systems overwrite yesterday's value with today's. That keeps the present tidy and makes every past decision impossible to judge fairly.
summary: Overwriting a record erases the reason behind a decision. Keeping history, with when it was true and when you learned it, makes the past fair to judge.
alt: An open notebook and a cup of coffee in morning light
caption: A notebook remembers the morning it was written. Most systems don't.
linkedin:
In March, a team made a reasonable call.
In September, it looks like a mistake.

Someone asks: why did we do that?

The honest answer is "because of what we knew in March."
But nobody can prove it. The system has been overwritten every day since.

Most records don't show what was known then. Only what is known now.

Full note in the comments.

Every fact has two dates, whether your systems keep them or not.

The date it became true in the world. A supplier's cost changed May 1.
The date you found out. The invoice arrived June 12.

The diagram shows a decision made on March 10, between both of them, with the information that was actually on the table.

Keep both dates and a review can ask the fair question: what did we believe at the time?

Three habits that make the past fair to judge:

1. When a value changes, keep the old one. Add, don't overwrite.
2. Record two dates: when it became true, and when you learned it.
3. In every review, start with "what did we know then?" before "what do we know now?"

You'll also start to see patterns in late information, like the vendor whose changes always reach you six weeks after they take effect.

A question for anyone who runs reviews or post-mortems:

How often does your team judge a past decision using information that didn't exist yet when it was made?

And what would change if you could see exactly what was known on the day?
